newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: POLL-Philippine June inflation seen at 4.26 pct.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Philippine June inflation seen at 4.26 pct.

text.p: Philippine inflation in June is expected to remain subdued, but dangers loom as the nation shields itself from the spillover effects of Thailand's financial woes, economists said on Thursday.

Five brokerages polled by Reuters forecast June inflation at 4.26 percent, almost steady from the previous month's figure and a 10-year low of 4.2 percent. Inflation in the year-earlier period was 9.8 percent.
The Philippine Central Bank said on Monday it expected June inflation to be much lower at 3.9 percent.
Analysts said prices may rise in the coming months as a result of a possible peso depreciation in line with the Thai baht's de facto devaluation.
Also a scheduled cut of one percentage point in the reserve requirement for banks on July 4 would increase liquidity and raise prices, they said.

"There's a need for the peso to realign itself with the baht. If they (the authorities) do not allow a depreciation, they will have to keep interest rates high," said Joven Babaan, an analyst of SBC Warburg.
Thailand on Wednesday began a managed float of its currency, which ended an exchange rate system that tied the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
The Philippine Central Bank on Wednesday had to raise its key rate by nine percentage points to 24 percent and sell dollars to protect the peso from attack arising from Thailand's woes.
In recent months, the Philippines had to grapple with investors' fears that it may become the next Thailand, where an over-heated property sector had hurt its banking industry.
Babaan warned that a depreciation of the peso of more than five percent may trigger a reversal in prices. Less than that would be manageable and will not impact badly on inflation, he said.
"Because the baht was devalued finally, the speculation will fade away (on the peso), said Luz Lorenzo, economist of Peregrine Securities.
She also dismissed concerns that a liquidity expansion from the reserve cut may lead to higher inflation.
"In fact, monetary policy has been contractionary. We've been having high real interest rates because of the Thai speculation even if inflation is low," Lorenzo pointed out.
Analysts said higher tuition fees and school supplies may raise June inflation. The education portion of the consumer price index contributes to 2.2 percent of the index.

DBS Securities economist Al Rillo, who projected the highest inflation among those polled, said he expected June to reflect the build-up of inflationary pressures on commodity prices with the approach of the lean months of the harvest season, which starts in July and ends in September.
Following are the projections made by five securities firms (in percentage terms):
Belson Prime Securities 4.0-4.1
DBS Securities 4.4-4.6
F. Yap Securities 4.2
Peregrine Securities 4.0-4.5
SBC Warburg 4.3
Average 4.26
